questions.stem: An engineer executes the command `kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080`. Based on the provided output, what is the distribution of HTTP response codes received?

options.text: 19 requests returned code 200 and 1 request returned code 503.
20 requests returned code 200 and 0 requests returned code 503.
10 requests returned code 200 and 10 requests returned code 503.
18 requests returned code 200 and 2 requests returned code 503.

questions.explanation: The output for the command with `-c 2` explicitly states `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. This indicates that out of the 20 total calls, 19 were successful and 1 triggered the circuit breaker with a 503 error.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect. The output clearly shows one instance of `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`, so not all requests were successful.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. The output shows 19 successful requests, not 10. The 50% split is not supported by the data.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect. The output shows only one 503 error, not two. The count for code 200 is 19, not 18.

It indicates that the echo-service is completely down.
It indicates that the Kubernetes pod is restarting.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect. The Fortio client continues to run and report statistics; it does not crash.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. The service is not completely down, as some requests (or in the first test, most) still return 200, and the 503 is specifically linked to the circuit breaker, not total unavailability.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect. There is no mention of pod restarts in the output or explanation.

questions.stem: A network engineer is configuring Cilium to protect a node against Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. They require the BPF program to execute at the earliest possible point in the networking driver, directly on the packet data before any other processing occurs, to drop malicious traffic. Which BPF hook should they use?

options.text: Traffic Control Ingress
XDP
Socket operations
Socket send/recv

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the XDP BPF hook is at the earliest point possible in the networking driver and triggers a run of the BPF program upon packet reception. It explicitly mentions that this hook is ideal for running filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic and other common DDOS protection mechanisms.

optionRationale.a: The Traffic Control Ingress hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, which is later than the XDP hook.
optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a specific cgroup and runs on TCP events, not at the earliest point in the networking driver for general packet reception.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, which is specific to TCP and not the earliest point for general packet processing.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote: The XDP BPF hook is at the earliest point possible in the networking driver and triggers a run of the BPF program upon packet reception. This achieves the best possible packet processing performance since the program runs directly on the packet data before any other processing can happen. This hook is ideal for running filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic, and other common DDOS protection mechanisms.

To the TC ingress hook of the host side of the veth pair
To the XDP hook of the physical network interface
To the socket operations hook of the root cgroup

optionRationale.a: The excerpt specifies the host side of the veth pair for monitoring traffic exiting the container, not the container side.
optionRationale.c: The XDP hook is used for prefiltering and DDoS protection at the driver level, not specifically for enforcing policy on traffic exiting a container via the veth pair.
optionRationale.d: The socket operations hook is used for monitoring TCP state transitions, not for enforcing policy on all traffic exiting a container via the veth pair.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote: By attaching to the TC ingress hook of the host side of this veth pair Cilium can monitor and enforce policy on all traffic exiting a container.

questions.stem: A network engineer deploys two `netperf` Pods to verify bandwidth enforcement. The server Pod has the annotation `kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M"`. The client Pod initiates a connection using `iperf3 -R -c <server_ip>`. Based on the provided test results, what is the observed behaviour of the traffic?

options.text: The egress traffic from the server Pod is limited to approximately 10 Mbit/s, as indicated by the receiver bitrate.
The ingress traffic to the server Pod is limited to 10 Mbit/s, as the client is receiving data.
The bandwidth limit is not enforced because the `netperf` Pods are on different nodes.
The egress traffic is limited to 20 Mbit/s because the ingress annotation takes precedence in reverse mode.

questions.explanation: The scenario describes testing egress bandwidth using `iperf3 -R` (reverse mode), where the remote host (server) sends data. The excerpt shows the output where the receiver bitrate is around 9.59 Mbits/sec, and explicitly states: 'As can be seen, egress traffic of the netperf-server Pod has been limited to 10Mbit per second.'

optionRationale.b: The test described uses `iperf3 -R`, which tests egress from the server (remote host sending). The excerpt confirms this is an egress test, not an ingress test.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode, and the test was performed with Pods on different nodes (implied by the anti-affinity and the context of verifying enforcement), successfully showing the limit.
optionRationale.d: The annotation set was `egress-bandwidth: "10M"` and `ingress-bandwidth: "20M"`. The test was for egress, so the 10M limit applies, not the 20M ingress limit.

questions.stem: An engineer is configuring a Cilium node with 60 GiB of total system memory. They set the flag `--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio` to `0.0025`. Based on the provided data, what is the calculated maximum number of entries for the Cilium connection tracking tables on this node?
questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium calculates the number of entries based on total memory with a minimum of 131072. The table shows that for a node with 60 GiB of memory and a ratio of 0.0025, the Cilium CT entries are 569120. questions.stem: You run two clusters joined by Cluster Mesh. A global Service named rebel-base already exists, and in cluster 1 you run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=local --overwrite`. You then curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1 while healthy backends exist in both clusters. What do you observe?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only, because the local backends are preferred while they remain healthy.
The replies come from pods in both clusters, because a global Service always balances across every cluster.
The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only, because the annotation pushes traffic away from the local cluster.
No replies arrive until the annotation is removed, because the local preference blocks remote endpoints permanently.

questions.explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to local makes the Global Service prefer healthy backends in the local cluster. Remote endpoints are used only as a fallback, so a client in cluster 1 keeps being served by cluster 1 pods for as long as those backends are available and healthy.

optionRationale.b: This is the behaviour without any affinity preference; the local value deliberately overrides it while local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: That is the effect of the remote value, not the local value.
optionRationale.d: Remote endpoints are not blocked permanently; they are used if and only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to know which namespaces in the cluster have had network flows during the past hour, so that they can narrow down where to start troubleshooting. Which Observer service RPC endpoint should they call?

options.text: `GetNamespaces`
`GetNodes`
`ServerStatus`
`GetFlows`

questions.explanation: `GetNamespaces` is the endpoint that reports namespaces which had network flows within the last one hour, which is exactly the time-bounded list the engineer needs. `GetNodes` reports per-Hubble-instance metrics and other information, `ServerStatus` summarises that same node information, and `GetFlows` streams flow events rather than listing namespaces.

optionRationale.b: ``GetNodes`` returns a list of metrics and other information related to each Hubble instance, not a list of namespaces with recent flows.
optionRationale.c: ``ServerStatus`` returns a summary of the information in ``GetNodes``, so it describes Hubble instances rather than namespaces.
optionRationale.d: ``GetFlows`` returns a stream of flow related events; it does not produce a list of namespaces active in the last hour.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster has WireGuard transparent encryption enabled. Two pods that are both scheduled on the same node exchange traffic with each other, and an engineer watching the node's traffic expects to see that traffic protected by the WireGuard tunnel. What does Cilium actually do with these packets?

options.text: It leaves them unencrypted, because traffic destined to the same node it was sent from is deliberately not encrypted.
It encrypts them, because WireGuard is enabled cluster-wide for every Cilium-managed endpoint.
It encrypts them only when the two pods belong to different namespaces.
It drops them unless a CiliumNetworkPolicy explicitly allows pod-to-pod traffic on that node.

questions.explanation: WireGuard encryption in Cilium covers traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes. When the source and the destination are the same node, the packets are not encrypted, and the excerpt states that this behaviour is intended: the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway, so encryption would provide no benefit.

optionRationale.b: Enabling WireGuard does not encrypt every packet; the same-node case is explicitly excluded from encryption.
optionRationale.c: Namespace membership plays no part in the decision — the criterion given is whether the traffic is destined to the node it was sent from.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about dropping same-node traffic; it says such packets are simply not encrypted.

citations.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
citations.quote:
Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which
they were sent. This behavior is intended.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a Cilium cluster whose nodes are spread across several routing domains, and the routers in the underlying network have no knowledge of the cluster's PodCIDRs. According to the excerpt, what does the encapsulation model require of that underlying network?

options.text: The underlying network must be configured with the PodCIDRs so that its routers can forward pod traffic.
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant, provided the cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.
All cluster nodes must sit within a single link-layer domain for encapsulated traffic to flow.
The PodCIDR size must be chosen to fit within the addressing limitations of the underlying network.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists simplicity as an advantage of the model: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs, and cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains. The only requirement stated is reachability between nodes using IP/UDP, which makes the underlying topology irrelevant. Options a, c and d each contradict a specific statement in the excerpt.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains, so a single link-layer domain is not required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the addressing space does not depend on any underlying networking limitations, so the PodCIDR need not be fitted to them.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant as long as
  cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.stem: In Cilium's encapsulation model, what purpose does the excerpt give for carrying the source security identity as metadata in the network packet?

options.text: It encrypts the packet payload between the cluster nodes.
It is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.
It lets the remote node learn the PodCIDR of the sending node.
It removes the need for cluster nodes to reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that encapsulation protocols allow metadata to be carried along with the network packet, and that Cilium uses this to transfer metadata such as the source security identity. It then states that this identity transfer is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node. The other options describe functions the excerpt does not attribute to the identity transfer.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes metadata transfer for the source security identity, not encryption of the payload.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link the identity transfer to PodCIDR discovery; it concerns the source security identity.
optionRationale.d: Node reachability over IP/UDP is described separately as a property of the model, not as something the identity transfer removes.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The identity transfer is an optimization
  designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.

questions.stem: An operator holds CAP_SYS_ADMIN in their own current user namespace and uses pod exec to enter a running Cilium agent container. Under what condition does this amount to privileged access?

options.text: Only if CAP_SYS_ADMIN is also held in the Cilium user namespace, which is the initial namespace.
Only if the operator also holds CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the Cilium container.
Always, because the Linux kernel permits joining other namespaces by default.
Only if the Cilium agent's volumes were mounted with unsafe options.

questions.explanation: The kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, so entering the Cilium container requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the current user namespace and the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace). When both namespaces carry that capability, the access is already privileged. Holding CAP_NET_ADMIN, kernel defaults or volume mount options play no part in this test.

optionRationale.b: CAP_NET_ADMIN is not the capability named in the excerpt; the test is CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so mount options are not the deciding factor.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: To enter the Cilium container, the ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN`` capability is required in both the current user namespace and in the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace).
